en: The *Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Sūtra Asked by Maitreya Bodhisattva), Fascicle One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, he was together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, as well as ten thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and others.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
I now wish to ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, about a few matters.
I wonder, World-Honored One,
whether you will grant me permission to do so?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying: “Maitreya,
ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, whatever you desire in your mind.”
"I shall analyze and explain it for you, so as to bring joy to your heart.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Thus we pray and desire to hear:

World-Honored One, how many dharmas must Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish so that they do not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, do not fall back or turn away from the dharma of supreme progress, subdue all demonic adversaries while practicing the bodhisattva conduct, know the intrinsic nature and characteristics of all dharmas as they truly are, and have no weariness of mind toward any world? Because their minds are unwearied, they do not rely on the wisdom of others, but swiftly accomplish *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva,
saying: “Excellent, excellent, Maitreya!”
"It is well that you are now able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such a profound meaning.
The Buddha again addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying:
"You should now listen with single-minded attention; I shall analyze and explain this profound meaning for you."
At that moment, Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! It is so.”
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha again addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying: "Maitreya!"

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish eight dharmas, they do not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; they do not regress or turn back from the dharmas of superior progress; when practicing the bodhisattva conduct, they subdue all māras and hostile adversaries; they know the intrinsic nature and characteristics of all dharmas as they truly are; their minds do not grow weary regarding any worldly realm; and because their minds do not grow weary, they do not rely on the wisdom of others, but swiftly accomplish *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

What are these eight? Maitreya, they are: the bodhisattva mahāsattvas’ accomplishment of the profound mind; accomplishment of the mind of practice; accomplishment of the mind of relinquishment; accomplishment of the mind that skillfully knows the method of dedication; accomplishment of the mind of great loving-kindness; accomplishment of the mind of great compassion; accomplishment of skillful knowledge of means; and accomplishment of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
“Maitreya! How do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish the profound mind? Maitreya!”
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, upon hearing praise of the Buddha or disparagement of the Buddha, their minds remain ultimately firm and unshakable regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Upon hearing praise or disparagement of the Dharma, their mind remains ultimately firm and unshakable regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Upon hearing praise or disparagement of the Saṅgha, their mind remains ultimately firm and unshakable regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Maitreya! In this way, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish the profound mind (adhyāśaya). Maitreya!”
"How do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish the mind of practice? Maitreya!

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas distance themselves from killing, distance themselves from stealing, distance themselves from sexual misconduct, distance themselves from false speech, distance themselves from divisive speech, distance themselves from harsh speech, and distance themselves from frivolous speech."
“Maitreya! In this way, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish the mind of practice. Maitreya!”
How do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish the mind of relinquishment? Maitreya!

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are masters of relinquishment and masters of giving, bestowing upon śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, the poor, beggars, and those of lowly status whatever is required: clothing, food, bedding, and medicinal decoctions for the sick.
"Maitreya! Thus do these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish the mind of equanimity. Maitreya!"
How do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish the mind that skillfully knows the method of dedication? Maitreya!
If all the roots of goodness cultivated by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—namely, the actions of body, speech, and mind—are entirely dedicated toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Maitreya! Thus, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ultimately accomplished the mind that thoroughly understands the skillful means of dedication. Maitreya!”
"How do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish the mind of great loving-kindness? Maitreya!

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish the bodily action of great loving-kindness, ultimately accomplish the verbal action of great loving-kindness, and ultimately accomplish the mental action of great loving-kindness."
“Maitreya! In this way, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish the mind of great loving-kindness. Maitreya!”
"How do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish the mind of great compassion? Maitreya!
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish irreproachable bodily action, ultimately accomplish irreproachable verbal action, and ultimately accomplish irreproachable mental action."
"Maitreya! In this way, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish the mind of great compassion. Maitreya!"
"How do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas achieve proficiency in skillful means? Maitreya!
It is when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas thoroughly understand conventional truth, thoroughly understand ultimate truth, and thoroughly understand both truths."
"Maitreya! In this way, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ultimately accomplished the skillful knowledge of expedient means. Maitreya!"
"How do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish the perfection of wisdom?

Maitreya! If the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas realize it thus: 'Depending on this dharma, this dharma exists; depending on this dharma, this dharma arises'—namely, ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions becoming; becoming conditions birth; and birth conditions old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress—thus there is only this great mass of suffering that has arisen."

“Maitreya! Because this dharma does not exist, that dharma does not exist; because this dharma ceases, that dharma ceases. That is to say: with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease. In this way, there is only the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.”
“Maitreya! In this way, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish the perfection of wisdom. Maitreya!”

This is called the ultimate accomplishment of the eight dharmas by all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, whereby they do not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Within the dharmas of supreme progress, they neither regress nor turn back; while practicing the bodhisattva conduct, they subdue all Māras and hostile enemies. They know the intrinsic nature and characteristics of all dharmas as they truly are, and their minds do not grow weary of the various worlds. Because their minds do not grow weary, they do not rely on the wisdom of others, but swiftly accomplish *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, along with the other bodhisattvas-mahāsattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Treatise on the Sūtra of the Questions of Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, Scroll One. Homage to the World-Honored One Maitreya.
It is asked:
"For what reason did the Tathāgata preach this sūtra?"

He replied: "The four phrases beginning with 'renunciation' (tyāga) demonstrate the three kinds of merit consisting of giving, morality, and cultivation; these are dharmas shared by bodhisattvas, non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.

The four phrases beginning with 'the profound mind' (gambhīracitta) demonstrate that those same four dharmas are exclusively the practice of bodhisattvas and are not shared with non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas. For this reason, the Tathāgata spoke this sūtra."

The manifestation of generosity demonstrates the merit of giving; the manifestation of abstaining from killing and so forth demonstrates the merit of ethical discipline; and the two phrases beginning with "compassion" demonstrate the merit of cultivation. What is the meaning of this?

There are heterodox practitioners and ordinary worldlings who, due to being separated from virtuous friends, not hearing the true Dharma, improper reflection, and failing to practice according to the teachings, falsely cling to views such as eternalism, which serve as causes for accumulating karma; because their various fetters and latent tendencies mutually rely on one another to powerfully increase the causes of the world; because they stubbornly adhere to false attachments that definitively establish the causes of the world; because they are devoid of the vision of the true reality; because they lack the intention to benefit others; and because they are greedily attached to worldly pleasures.

"Although those non-Buddhists possess the seeds of wholesome roots such as giving, because of doubt and regret, the water of craving moistens their consciousness; abiding upon the ground of the five aggregates of clinging, covered by the soil of ignorance, and through the convergence of the seasons, they are able to produce the sprout of consciousness, which grows in succession to form the fruits of the world."

Furthermore, when śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas associate with virtuous friends—those who have already crossed the ocean of birth and death and those who wish to cross it—they hear teachings on the faults and afflictions of the world; moreover, through their own limited insight, they come to loathe worldly suffering and delight in the bliss of nirvāṇa. Desiring to abandon the world and seek the path to liberation, although they do not grasp at merits such as giving, they nevertheless do not depart from such merits, and are thus able to subdue the afflictions and attain the most excellent dharmas.

For this reason, although one may cultivate and accumulate virtuous dharmas such as giving (*dāna*), because of the absence of these four dharmas, one will not attain Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).

Furthermore, a bodhisattva ultimately fulfills and accomplishes eight dharmas: establishing great undertakings and bearing heavy burdens; drawing near to true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); deeply perceiving the faults and afflictions of the world and knowing the tranquility of *nirvāṇa*; not wearying of worldly suffering for the sake of sentient beings; because they do not lose the cause when first generating the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), they achieve the profound resolve (*adhyāśaya*);

relinquishing their own bodily pleasure for the benefit of sentient beings, they practice virtues such as giving and dedicate them toward Great Enlightenment; relying on the power of skillful means (*upāya*), they increase even small virtues such as giving; and they are able to protect themselves from falling into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.

Because they have attained the ultimate perfection of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are able to purify the merits of giving and other virtues, causing them to abide in the bodhisattva path. By manifesting the four phrases beginning with "the profound mind," they are able to encompass the four phrases beginning with "giving. These constitute the unique dharmas of a bodhisattva, through which one can attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*); for this reason, the Tathāgata preached this *sūtra*.
Question: "For what further reason did the Tathāgata preach this sūtra? Answer:
"To refute causelessness and inverted causes, and to accord with the correct cause and effect, the Tathāgata has spoken this sūtra.
What is the meaning of this?"
Regarding the statement that one does not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*: this is because the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*) has been accomplished. What does this clarify?

It means that when the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas perceive the *dharmadhātu*, they immediately and forever become free from the obstacles to the bodhicitta—namely, all afflictions such as the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*). Having transcended the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, they enter the rank of Bodhisattvas and arise in the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*). Because the cause of the bodhicitta is not lost, they realize the profound mind; for this reason, it is called "not regressing from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"Furthermore, it is said that they do not regress because they have realized the supreme Dharma.
What does this clarify?
It clarifies that they have accomplished the practice of giving."
What is the meaning of this?

Because one gives rise to the fundamental path of action characterized by a mind free from harm, one embraces the most supreme and excellent practices; therefore, one does not turn away from the fundamental path of action, and while practicing giving and other deeds, one does not regress in any situation. For this reason, it is called "non-retrogression."

Furthermore, regarding the statement that when practicing the bodhisattva path one subdues all māras and hostile adversaries, this is because of the accomplishment of the mind that skillfully knows the expedient means of dedication (pariṇāmanā).
What does this clarify?

Briefly stated, there are four māras: namely, the māra of afflictions (*kleśamāra*), the māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*), the māra of death (*mṛtyumāra*), and the celestial māra (*devaputramāra*). Of these, the māra of afflictions alone is the root; it is upon the māra of afflictions that the remaining three māras depend.

Why is this? Because the minds of ordinary worldlings are entangled by afflictions; relying on these minds thus entangled by afflictions, they delight in seeking worldly pleasure and dedicate practices such as giving toward rebirth in the heavenly realms.
For this reason, they are ensnared and bound by the Māra of the aggregates and the Māra of death, and remain subject to the celestial Māras.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva severs all afflictions such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and further distances himself from fears such as the inability to sustain life. Renouncing his own personal happiness for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, he cultivates and accumulates the roots of goodness and merit—such as compassion, loving-kindness, and generosity—and dedicates them all toward the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). Thus, remaining far removed from all Māras and evil paths, he is said to "subdue all Māras and hostile enemies" when practicing the conduct of a Bodhisattva.

"Furthermore, regarding the statement that 'the mind does not grow weary amidst all worlds,' this is because of the accomplishment of great loving-kindness and great compassion (*mahāmaitrī-mahākaruṇā*).
What does this clarify?

Because Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas constantly have their minds pierced by the arrows of ignorance of all sentient beings in the world and suffer mental affliction, yet through the accomplishment of great loving-kindness and great compassion, they regard the benefit of sentient beings as their own benefit. Consequently, great loving-kindness and great compassion arise, whereby they are able to benefit all sentient beings; for this reason, it is called 'the mind not growing weary amidst all worlds.'"
Furthermore, regarding the statement that one "knows the intrinsic nature and characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are," this is because of accomplishment through skillful means.
What does this clarify?
It clarifies that it is by knowing the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena.
What is the meaning of this?

Because bodhisattvas skillfully understand the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and skillfully understand the means of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), they do not adhere to the two extremes of existence and non-existence.
What does this clarify?
Although a bodhisattva perceives the objects of consciousness, they have already previously examined those objects of consciousness. Why is this so?

Because they never abandon the power of mind directed toward the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), they do not fall into the extreme view of existence; yet, while never abandoning the ultimate truth, they always skillfully understand the matters of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).

Why is this? Because they constantly and clearly perceive all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) without abandoning worldly thoughts, mental states, or verbal expressions; therefore, they do not fall into the attachment of the view of the infinite (*anantavāda*).
Because one is able to skillfully know these two kinds of meanings, one is therefore said to "know the intrinsic characteristics of all dharmas as they truly are.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "because the mind does not become weary, and because one does not rely on the wisdom of others, one swiftly accomplishes *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*," this is due to the accomplishment of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
What does this clarify?
It clarifies that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas observe conditioned phenomena through prajñā.
Furthermore, what is the meaning of this?

The Bodhisattva observes all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as being without a person, without a sentient being, without a master, and without autonomy; they arise through mutual dependence, increasing and gaining power, and based upon fundamental karma, they create all karmic actions. They are like the illusory figures created by a magician, performing various feats such as coming and going or leaping about without ever becoming weary. Therefore, it is said that this is "due to the mind not becoming weary."
Furthermore, the mind does not grow weary because it is free from the notion of a sentient being (*sattva*).
What does this clarify?

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely without reality; they exist only through the mutual dependence of various karmic forces acting as external powers, which are able to bring about the formation of all conditioned phenomena.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva knows that conditioned phenomena truly lack a self or soul; yet, without relying on the wisdom of others, they carry out whatever practices they undertake, accomplishing them all through the increase of the *vīryapāramitā* (perfection of vigor), and thereby swiftly realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seek sarvajñā (all-knowledge), they manifest the distancing from causelessness and inverted causes, and accord with correct causes and effects; for this reason, the Tathāgata has preached this sūtra.
Question: "For what further reason did the Tathāgata speak this sūtra? Answer:

"Because bodhisattvas of the indeterminate group seek the determinate group, [the Tathāgata] demonstrates how those bodhisattvas enter the stage of right determination by accomplishing which practices; he thus teaches this sūtra so that they may cultivate the practices of the true cause."
What is the meaning of this?

Although a bodhisattva may have cultivated and accumulated roots of goodness for immeasurable eons prior to realizing the correct position of the first stage (*bhūmi*), they have not yet attained the state of non-retrogression, nor have they reached the ultimate place free from fear; their mind is not yet settled, and they are constantly oppressed by the sufferings and afflictions of the world.

Because they have not yet attained the power of the root of bodhicitta—compassion—and have not yet attained superior power, they observe the twelve links of dependent origination through worldly path-wisdom. They contemplate conditioned formations as they truly are and, by relying on the worldly path, they contemplate the quiescent dharma-realm; however, because they lack the skillful means of wisdom in seeking great nirvāṇa, they fall to the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
If one falls into the stages of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha, there are three kinds of loss.
What are these three?
First, the retrogression and loss of all seeds of Mahāyāna roots of goodness.
Second, they fall away from the cause that can bring happiness to all sentient beings;
third, they fall away from the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
For this reason, the Tathāgata said in the sūtras:
"Kāśyapa! For example, although all the gods and humans in the world may polish a counterfeit lapis lazuli bead, that counterfeit bead can never become a genuine lapis lazuli gem."
In this way, Kāśyapa,

all śrāvakas who cultivate morality, concentration, and wisdom, as well as all virtues such as the dhūta practices, will ultimately never be able to sit at the site of enlightenment and achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Kāśyapa! It is like refining great vaidūrya; one can obtain immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of precious jewels according to one's wish.
In the same way, Kāśyapa!
"Because they cultivate the bodhisattva practices, they are able to give birth to all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, humans, and devas.
Based on this meaning, the Tathāgata stated in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* that there are four kinds of non-virtuous friends for a bodhisattva.
What are the four?
First, those seeking the state of a śrāvaka who desire only to deliver themselves;
second, those seeking the state of a pratyekabuddha who take delight in minor matters; [and so forth].
Third, reading non-Buddhist scriptures such as the Lokāyata;
fourth, practicing and studying all manner of literary embellishments.
Those who associate with these four things increase only worldly benefits, not the benefits of the Dharma.
Furthermore, in another sutra, the Venerable Kāśyapa addressed Mañjuśrī:

"There are those who have committed the five heinous crimes who can give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, cultivate various merits, and realize great enlightenment, whereas Arhats cannot."

For example, just as a person whose sense organs are destroyed is incapable of acting within the realms of the five desires and gains no benefit therefrom, so too do the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, having severed all fetters and afflictions, remain incapable of acting or gaining benefit regarding any of the Buddha-dharmas; they lack such power to observe the Buddha-dharmas.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī, it is all ordinary beings who repay the kindness of the Tathāgata, not the śrāvakas. Why is this?
Ordinary people, upon hearing of the Buddha’s merits, are able to resolve their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of ensuring that the lineage of the Three Jewels is not severed;

whereas *śrāvakas*, even if they were to hear of the various Buddha-dharmas such as the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses for the rest of their lives, are unable to resolve their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"O sons of the gods!
Those who have not yet resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should give rise to the great bodhicitta."
Having already entered the stage of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, they are unable to again resolve their minds toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? Because all Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and the like have severed the stream of birth and death, and are thus unable to take repeated births within the world.

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* perceive the ultimate truth within the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), they resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and, because they do not lose the cause, they attain the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*).

By means of the perfection of wisdom, one correctly embraces the cultivation of the practice of ethical discipline and so forth; being unattached to body or life and acting solely for the benefit of sentient beings, at the time of such cultivation, one is called an irreversible bodhisattva.
"You should know! Therefore, it is said in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*:

'When a bodhisattva gives rise to such a mind, he immediately transcends the stage of ordinary beings and enters the rank of bodhisattvas; he is born into the family of the Buddhas with a noble lineage, beyond reproach, surpassing all worldly paths, well-established in the bodhisattva-dharma, well-established in the true station of bodhisattvas, and enters into the reality (*tathatā*) that is equal throughout the three times.'"
Within the lineage of the Tathāgatas, they will certainly and ultimately attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
When a bodhisattva abides in such dharmas, it is called abiding in the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi).
"Because of the quality of immovability, one transcends the five fears— namely, the fear of lacking a livelihood,
the fear of ill repute, the fear of death, the fear of falling into evil realms, and the fear of being intimidated by a great assembly— and is completely freed from them all."
Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas are free from the marks of self and so forth.
Regarding "transcending the stage of ordinary beings," there are nine kinds of such transcendence.
One should know this!

Regarding "entering the stage of a bodhisattva," it refers to the transcendence of that stage; it is like the initial dwelling in the womb, because the dharma is analogous to the first moment of conception.

Regarding "being born into the family of the Buddhas," it refers to the transcendence of that family; it is because one is born into the family by relying on skillful means and *prajñā*, as the dharma is analogous to birth.
Regarding "noble lineage beyond reproach," this refers to the excellence of lineage; because it is born from the practice of the Mahāyāna, it is analogous to the nature of a son.
Regarding "surpassing all worldly paths," this refers to transcendence; because worldly paths cannot encompass the emergence of the path [to liberation], it is analogous to the nature of birth.

Regarding "entering the supramundane path," this refers to the transcendence of the [mundane] entry, because one enters the path by means of the supramundane path, thereby giving rise to a corresponding state of being.

Regarding "dwelling well within the Bodhisattva-dharma," this refers to the transcendence of the self, because taking great compassion as its essence, one regards the affairs of others as one's own, thereby giving rise to a corresponding state of being within one's own person.

Regarding the Bodhisattva’s skillful abiding in the right place: it is an abiding that transcends [the world], yet does not abandon the world; it is an abiding that is undefiled by skillful means; it is a skillful and correct abiding, because its mode of arising and its mode of abiding accord with the nature of phenomena.

Regarding those who enter the *tathatā* (suchness) of the equality of the three periods of time: they transcend karma because they accord with the noble wisdom of emptiness and give rise to dharmas that resemble [the state of] life; they are certain to attain ultimate *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* within the lineage of the Tathāgata because they transcend the ultimate [state], the non-interruption of the Buddha-lineage, and the ultimate *nirvāṇa*, as these resemble the accomplishment of the Path.

In this way, he manifests the birth of ordinary beings and the birth of bodhisattvas, which are dissimilar in their entry into the womb because one is with defilement and the other is without defilement. Likewise, they are dissimilar in sequence; dissimilar in family; dissimilar in lineage; dissimilar in emergence; dissimilar in entry; dissimilar in body; dissimilar in location; dissimilar in the activities of birth; and dissimilar in accomplishment.
Thus the Venerable Vasubandhu has explained the ultimate accomplishment of the mind.
Other masters of the treatises provide a different interpretation of the phenomena,
stating in verse:
“What kind of mind does a bodhisattva mahāsattva give rise to that perceives the world as illusory?
The Buddha has taught that it is this initial mind.”
"What does this clarify? It clarifies that those who perceive the world as illusory do so because all worlds arise solely from causes and conditions and possess no substantial reality.
As the Venerable Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna stated in verse:"
"Arising from the conjunction of causes and conditions, those phenomena have no substantial reality.
If they lack substantial reality, how can they be called 'existent dharmas'?"
In the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Akṣayamati said:
"One observes the wisdom of skillful means regarding causes and conditions, knowing that all phenomena arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions."

If all phenomena arise in dependence upon causes, in dependence upon conditions, and in dependence upon their combination, then those phenomena do not depend upon a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
If a phenomenon is not a self, not a person, and not a life-span, then that phenomenon cannot be reckoned as past, present, or future.
"If a bodhisattva can observe in this way, it is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s wisdom of skillful means in observing the conjunction of causes and conditions.
What is the meaning of "not relying on a self"?
It arises in dependence upon various causes and conditions, not in dependence upon a self, because there is no real essence of a self.

It is like fire produced from various conditions: the nature of fire is heat, yet this heat has no substantial reality; nevertheless, through the conjunction of causes and conditions, it is designated that "fire has heat."
In this way, one does not perceive a real self external to the body-faculty, because such a self lacks substantial reality.
As for this lack of substantial reality: is it like space, or is it like conditioned phenomena?
If it were identical to empty space, it would be a non-entity;
if it were identical to conditioned phenomena, it would be impermanent.
Terms such as "self," "person," "sentient being," and "life-span" are various names used for the sake of converting sentient beings; they do not refer to a real, substantial self.

Furthermore, as stated in the sūtra, in the chapter on the dialogue between the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati and the noble Brahmaviśeṣacintin regarding the accomplishment of all Buddha-dharmas, it is said in verse:
"All phenomena arise from causes and conditions; Those phenomena have no substantial reality.
If phenomena have no real substance, Then those phenomena do not truly arise."
"The Bodhisattva knows that sentient beings are thus without a limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi);
by relying on the wisdom of that limit of reality, he knows the emptiness or substantiality of all phenomena.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva knows that all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, and that sentient beings have no real substance.

If it is thus, the mind-consciousness of all the world is entirely false conceptualization; that bodhisattva’s mind, which is the practice of unimpeded wisdom in the equality of the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) regarding all phenomena, is itself the initial mind. Therefore, this is called the first generation of the mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, the verse says:
"He does not perceive the stage of ordinary beings, Because its essence is empty;
For this reason, the Buddhas declare That he has transcended the stage of ordinary beings."
"Those who distance themselves from the Dharma of the Noble Ones, who are stained by attachment to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth,
and who dwell amidst the five desires and the necessities of life— therefore they are called 'ordinary persons' (*pṛthagjana*). What does this clarify?
As for "ground" (*bhūmi*): that place where ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are born is called the ground of ordinary persons.
This is the place within the three realms bound by afflictions (*kleśa*), arising in dependence upon afflictions; it is called the ground of ordinary persons.

Therefore, that initial mind perceives the three realms as entirely empty and does not give rise to the conceptualization of a single dharma. Because it does not give rise to the conceptualization of a single dharma, it does not desire or take pleasure in birth in any place.
Except for the compassionate mind intended to transform and guide all sentient beings, they constantly contemplate the tranquil nature of reality.
For this reason, it is said that those bodhisattvas have transcended the stage of ordinary beings.
Therefore, the verse says:
"Because the essence of phenomena does not exist, they are empty; because they are empty, there is nothing to be done.
Since they are free from all marks, the wise have nothing to seek."
Regarding "entering the stage of a bodhisattva," the verse says:
"Emptiness itself is called bodhi; The Buddha taught that afflictions are a disease, As well as falling into the stage of a pratyekabuddha And grasping at the rank of a śrāvaka."
“Regarding ‘emptiness itself is called bodhi’: to realize, as it truly is, that sentient beings are empty is called bodhi.

For this reason, the noble Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, in his discourse on the four foundations of mindfulness, said: ‘When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the contemplation of dharmas, if they perceive all dharmas as being apart from emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-action, non-arising, and non-origination, and as being apart from the twelve links of dependent origination, this is not called realization as it truly is.’”

If one does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon as being apart from emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-activity, non-arising, non-origination, and apart from the twelve links of dependent origination.
If a bodhisattva can thus awaken to the fact that all sentient beings have no substantial reality, this is called awakening according to reality.
Therefore, the verse says: "Emptiness itself is named bodhi."

Therefore, if a bodhisattva of the first stage realizes that all sentient beings are empty and, abandoning the benefit of all sentient beings, takes up the state of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, this is called the affliction to be remedied by a bodhisattva of the first stage.
Therefore, the verse says: "The Buddha taught that the afflictions are a disease, because they cause one to fall to the stage of a pratyekabuddha and to take up the position of a śrāvaka.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"Knowing emptiness and being free from the two extremes, there is no duality; this is nirvāṇa."
"Because it is untainted by nirvāṇa, the Buddha spoke of the bodhisattva stage.
What is the meaning of "knowing emptiness and being free from the two extremes"?
As it is said in the *Tathāgatadharmamudrā-sūtra*:
Śāriputra said: "That which is the dharma of non-differentiation is precisely what is called emptiness. Śāriputra said:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding that which is called ‘emptiness,’ what does this term signify?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"That which is called 'emptiness' is neither expressible nor inexpressible.
Since it is neither expressible nor inexpressible, it cannot be represented."
If it cannot be manifested, it is neither mundane nor supramundane.
Because it is neither mundane nor supramundane, it is called "empty."
If one can thus understand emptiness, it is called being free from the two extremes.
If a bodhisattva is free from those two extremes, they do not fall into afflictions, nor do they grasp at the two kinds of nirvana—those of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"The Buddha said that those who have the disease of afflictions do so because they grasp at the characteristics of different stages (*bhūmi*).
To grasp at the characteristics of different stages means to grasp at the characteristics of the different stages of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and so forth."

It is also called "abandoning the benefit of sentient beings," because one has grasped the bliss of unconditioned *nirvāṇa*, and because it obstructs the *bodhi* of a Buddha. Furthermore, there is another meaning:

"being free from the disease of afflictions" means being separated from the disease of afflictions, because one does not grasp the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), but rather, by virtue of the power of one's original vow, does not abandon the benefit of all sentient beings.

If it is thus, there is neither the illness of the two vehicles nor the illness of afflictions; practicing all phenomena as empty in accordance with reality—this is called the entry of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas into the bodhisattva stage.

Because they have distanced themselves from all afflictions and distanced themselves from all remedial dharmas, such bodhisattvas, through non-dual practice and by the power of their original vows, do not abandon the benefit of sentient beings; thus, they do not fall into the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor are they defiled by worldly afflictions.

This is the most difficult and unsurpassed task of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas: although they do not perceive any sentient beings, they practice all the various deeds for the sake of sentient beings. Such a matter is inconceivable; it cannot be understood by any in the world, it is the most rare and marvelous thing, and it is something that all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are unable to see.
"For this reason, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Nāgārjuna spoke a verse in the *Bodhicittotpādana-śāstra* (Treatise on the Accumulation of the Merits of Bodhi):
'This is a most rare occurrence, The foremost inconceivable thing:
The Bodhisattva practices the deeds [of a bodhisattva], Yet does not perceive a sentient being.'"
"The Tathāgata has also spoken thus in order to praise the truly rare merits of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as they truly are.
As stated in the sūtras, there are four kinds of true merits of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."
What are these four?
First, being able to believe in and understand emptiness while also believing in cause and effect;
second, knowing that all phenomena are devoid of a self, yet giving rise to great compassion for sentient beings.
Third, they deeply delight in nirvana yet wander within saṃsāra;
fourth, all their deeds and practices are performed solely for the sake of sentient beings without seeking any karmic reward—if one acts in this way, they are born into the family of the Buddha.
Therefore, the verse says:
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, By being free from all afflictions,
Then realize the stage of a bodhisattva, And thus are born into the family of the Buddha.”
"What does this clarify? Furthermore, as for those of the Buddha-family, what dharmas must they practice to be born into the family of the Tathāgata?
It means: because of being free from afflictions, because of understanding the practice of emptiness, and because of knowing one's own station."

Furthermore, because they perform deeds that benefit sentient beings and because they do not lose their way in practice, they attain such a Dharma as this, which is called a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva being born into the family of the Buddha.
"What does this clarify?
The verse says:
'The Buddha taught that the Tathāgata-family consists of skillful means and prajñā.'"
"When a Bodhisattva is born into such a family, for this reason they are not to be disparaged.
What is the meaning of this?
To speak of "skillful means" (upāya) is, in brief, to never abandon any sentient being.
That which is called "prajñā" refers to the non-appropriation of all dharmas.

These two kinds of dharmas constitute the family of all Buddhas; therefore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is born from skillful means and prajñā, because he is sustained by these two dharmas of skillful means and prajñā.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas appear in the world out of a desire to benefit all sentient beings, yet in reality they do not arise based on afflictions or karma.
Being thus, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot be censured; they remain far removed from all qualities that the devas and others might criticize, and are born into the supreme family of the Buddhas.
For this reason, one’s noble lineage cannot be subject to reproach or disparagement.
Therefore, in the Sūtras, the Tathāgata spoke these verses for the sake of the Brahmins:
“Gods, humans, gandharvas, Nāgas, yakṣas, and flocks of birds...”
All such karmas as these have been completely extinguished.
Those outflows have been scattered and brought to an end; like a lotus, they remain unstained.
If one can understand it thus, one will not be defiled by any desires.
"Thus, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is called a true son of the Buddha, not a different kind of son such as those of the devas.
Therefore, the verse says:
The bodhisattva knows the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), And practices the perfections (*pāramitā*)."
"Because they have attained the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga), they transcend the world.
What does it mean for a bodhisattva to know the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)?
It means that all phenomena (dharma) are entirely quiescent (śānta).
Therefore, the Tathāgata spoke this verse:
"All phenomena are without essence, For in reality there are no things;
Because they are neither born nor extinguished, They are named the Reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi)."

"In this way, the *prajñāpāramitā* knows that all phenomena are without essence and are the true limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Through the *prajñāpāramitā*, one knows the practice of the path of cessation; through the five *pāramitās*, one knows the path of skillful means and merit."
In this way, by means of these merits and wisdom, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to attain the enlightenment of a Buddha, exhaust all afflictions, and benefit sentient beings.
"Furthermore, one cultivates the various pāramitās while also knowing them according to the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi).
How does one know this?
By not perceiving the three factors—the giver, the recipient, and the material gift—one practices the pure pāramitās."
When a bodhisattva practices the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) in this manner, they are therefore untainted (*anāsrava*); being untainted, they transcend all worldly paths.
Thus, the verse says:
"Distinguishing worldly conduct within the dense forest of afflictions,"
"Transcending the worldly state is the entry into the supramundane path.
Regarding the practitioner who discriminates the world, there are briefly two kinds of discrimination:
first, discrimination of reality, such as the notion that "form has the characteristic of being visible," and so forth; [second, discrimination of non-reality].
Second is the superior discrimination, namely the blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth within that very form.
"The world" refers to the afflictions of the five aggregates;
"the thicket" is deep, precipitous, dark, terrifying, and fearsome—unobservable, difficult to see, and difficult to know.

"In this way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva observes his own body, analyzing it, analyzing it excellently, and analyzing it according to the five aggregates; he does not cling to the matters previously described, and reflects thus:
'How shall I cause sentient beings to understand? "
Therefore, the verse says:
"Knowing all phenomena as they truly are, The reality transcends the aggregates, the one, and the two;
If one does not perceive the affairs of sentient beings, How can one transform sentient beings?"
"The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva, practicing untainted wisdom as well as meritorious deeds, proceeds toward the supramundane path.
"For this reason, the Bodhisattva enters the supramundane path."
Question: "How does one dwell well within the Dharma of a bodhisattva? Answer:
The verse says:
"Entering the various stages of the bodhisattvas, dwelling securely within their own dharma,
and relying upon supernormal powers and masteries, they transform all sentient beings."
"Regarding 'entering the various stages of a bodhisattva,' it is as the sutra says:
'Because of thoroughly knowing the progressive transition from stage to stage.
Regarding 'transforming all sentient beings,' it is as the sutra says:"
"Because one attains a hundred samādhis, up to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas that cannot be calculated or known.
Regarding the attainment of mastery, as it is said concerning various merits, at what time does this occur?
What are the dharmas? What is mastery?
What are the accomplished matters?
What is their practice?

It is the attainment of mastery over all things and the non-retrogression of the seeds of all Buddha-dharmas; because they accomplish all Buddha-dharmas, it is said that they "abide well within the Bodhisattva-dharma."
Question: "How does a bodhisattva dwell properly in the right state? Answer:
The verse says: "At one time, in the presence of all Buddhas, having heard, retained, contemplated, cultivated, and explained [the teachings],
they achieved mastery in practice and realization, as well as perfect enlightenment, offerings, and so forth."
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices such dharmas as these, it is called 'dwelling securely' within the proper station of a bodhisattva.
Therefore, the sutra says: "The bodhisattva dwells well in the proper station."
Question: "How does one enter into the true suchness (*tathatā*) that is equal throughout the three periods of time? Answer:
The verse says:
"Knowing the bodhi of all Buddhas, as well as the practices of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
and knowing that the three periods of time of the Buddhas are empty— this is called the entry of good intention."
"What is the meaning of this?
It means knowing that the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas of the three periods of time is equal.

Furthermore, it means being able to know that because all Buddhas rely upon the *rūpakāya*, they practice all the deeds of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; and it means knowing that all phenomena of the past, future, and present arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions and possess no substantial reality."

As for entering with a wholesome mind: as previously explained, one knows that all phenomena of the three periods of time are equal and non-dual; one enters by knowing them as they truly are—of a single flavor, an equal flavor—without destroying them.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"One enters into the dharma of the suchness that is equal throughout the three periods of time.
A question is asked:
“How is it that one is certain to attain ultimate *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* within the lineage of the Tathāgata?
He replied: “The verse says:”
“The Bodhisattva purifies afflictions, And purifies the minds of sentient beings;
Endowed with great compassion, He will certainly attain enlightenment.
What is the meaning of “the Bodhisattva purifies afflictions”?

Because the afflictions such as the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which are to be abandoned on the first stage, are all completely distanced during the period of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), those afflictions are abandoned within that path of seeing.
As previously stated, one sees all phenomena as equal throughout the three periods of time, as explained in the *Tathatā-sūtra*.
Regarding the purification of the minds of sentient beings, it is as the subsequent sūtra says:
"In a single moment, one transforms and guides a hundred sentient beings; or, through the sovereign power of one's vows, even more."
Thus, these are attained by means of purifying all afflictions through the power of transformative instruction.
Therefore, the sutra below says:
"For this reason, I shall first abide in wholesome dharmas, and also cause others to abide in wholesome dharmas."

Why is this? If a person does not practice virtue themselves and is not endowed with virtuous conduct, it is impossible for them to teach the Dharma to others so that those others may abide in the wholesome Dharma.
Because they have attained the mind of great kindness and great compassion, the aforementioned sutra states:

"This mind takes great compassion as its primary focus; therefore, the Bodhisattva purifies their own afflictions and purifies the minds of sentient beings, fully possessing great kindness and compassion, which is called ultimately attaining Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi."
Because they proceed with certainty toward great enlightenment, the verse says:
"The Son of the Buddha, Vajragarbha, Speaks of ten dharmas for the initial mind;
This is called the Buddha’s bodhi, Because it ultimately perfects the Buddha-way."
"What is the meaning of this?

Because the noble Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha has taught these ten kinds of dharmas as the untainted bodhicitta of the first stage of a bodhisattva, and because these ten kinds of mind are themselves called the Buddha-bodhi, it is said that they are ultimately *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Furthermore, a verse says:
"Just as a good seed Is able to produce stems, leaves, and so forth,
So too is the bodhicitta No different from all the Buddha-dharmas."
"What is the meaning of this?
It is because the mind that first realizes the Dharma serves as the seed for all Buddha-dharmas, and because the dharmas of the first stage serve as the cause for all Buddha-dharmas."
Furthermore, a verse says:
"The mind increases in the first stage; The Buddha has taught this as the various stages.
For the most wondrous and supreme Bodhisattva, He speaks of the new moon as a metaphor."
"What does this clarify? As it is said in a verse from the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-bodhicitta-sūtra*:
'Just as when the moon first appears, It waxes until it becomes the full moon;'"
"In this manner, the Ground of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi) increases, and that is itself the Buddha.
One should know that these ten points have been interpreted differently by other masters of the treatises.
Therefore, for the sake of leading bodhisattvas of the indeterminate group toward the state of the determinate group, the Tathāgata has preached this sūtra.
*Maitreyaparipṛcchāsūtra-śāstra*, Fascicle One. *Maitreyaparipṛcchāsūtra-śāstra*, Fascicle Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Later Wei Dynasty.
Question: "By what meaning is one called 'non-retrogressive'? Answer:

"Because all bodhisattvas have realized the cause of certainty upon reaching the first stage (*bhūmi*), from that point until they attain Buddhahood, they constantly practice according to reality with a profound mind, causing the bodhicitta to increase progressively."
"Because the dharmas that are to be countered cannot obstruct him, he is called 'non-retrogressive. Question:
"Furthermore, by what meaning is he called 'non-retrogressive regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi'?"
He replied: "Because one has attained the causes for non-retrogression, namely the eight dharmas such as the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*).

Furthermore, because all afflictions, such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and craving, which are contrary to the state of non-retrogression, have been entirely abandoned through the power of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*)."
Furthermore, all afflictions such as the view of a self-body have followed ignorance since beginningless time and cannot be abandoned;

because they grasp at causes such as self and pleasure, and are devoid of the skillful means of prajñā, they are oppressed by the sufferings of the world and abandon the benefit of all sentient beings to seek their own nirvana.

Therefore, when a bodhisattva attains the profound mind of compassion, they remain far removed from the causes of attachment to self and pleasure; possessing skillful means and wisdom (*upāya-prajñā*), although they are pressed by the sufferings of the world, they do not abandon the work of benefiting sentient beings. By severing the root of afflictions such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), they at that time attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, the noble Ajita said:
"That mind arises free from all afflictions," and so forth.

Question: "If being free from afflictions such as the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is called the cause of non-retrogression, then both Bodhisattvas and Srotāpannas are equally free from afflictions such as the view of a self-body."
"Why is it that bodhisattvas do not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, whereas those such as *srotāpannas* do regress?
He replied: "It is because of the differences in their mental activities (*citta-carita*)."
What does this clarify?
It clarifies that from the time they first resolve their minds, there are all manner of distinctions in the mental activities and characteristics of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas.
In what way are they distinguished?

Śrāvakas are unable to cultivate the causes for benefiting others; therefore, they abandon the welfare of sentient beings to seek their own nirvāṇa. Seeing that those within the three realms are scorched by the fires of afflictions such as greed and oppressed by impermanence, they develop weary detachment toward the three realms as if their own bodies or clothes were ablaze. Contemplating the conditioned formations of the five aggregates, such as impermanence, they eventually sever the fetters of the three realms. Only then do they eliminate afflictions such as greed, gradually attenuating them until they transcend the three realms.
Because Bodhisattvas have attained the profound mind (*gambhīracitta*), they always delight in benefiting all the world and perform deeds for the welfare of all sentient beings.

Although they are oppressed by the sufferings of the world, because they have perfected the power of skillful means (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), they are able to practice the path of the Śrāvaka as it truly is, yet they do not realize the fruit of the Śrāvaka path.
This is because one has previously severed those obstructing factors that lead to the state of a śrāvaka.
What are these factors that lead to the state of a śrāvaka? They are:
the abandonment of the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and the inability to increase the practices of great compassion and so forth.
If bodhisattvas attain the practices of the profound resolve and its associated dharmas that attend the bodhicitta, they can act as the cause for realizing the stage of awakening.
At that time, because the bodhisattva perceives all phenomena, they are able to increase the power of the bodhicitta and skillfully seek out matters that benefit all sentient beings.

At that time, one directly perceives the reality of the dharma-realm; by perceiving the dharma-realm, one immediately distances oneself from all afflictions to be abandoned through the path of vision and attains the ultimate bodhicitta.
As it is said in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*:
"The bodhisattva-mahāsattva generates such a mind; this mind has great compassion as its foremost [quality]. And so forth.

Once that bodhisattva has thus realized and seen the Path, they skillfully seek to benefit all sentient beings. By virtue of having well-cultivated the dharma of the profound mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and other such qualities, they are free from self-interest and pleasure, and are not burned by the fires of affliction (*kleśa*), because their nature is dissimilar [to that of ordinary beings]. Since the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva constantly practices with a profound mind for the sake of benefiting others, at the very moment of seeing the Path, they sever all afflictions within the three realms. In contrast, the Śrāvakas and others have not previously cultivated the skillful means of compassion; therefore, they lack the practice of benefiting others and only attain Arhatship after gradually severing their afflictions.
"For this reason, it is said in the *Sāgaramati-bodhisattva-sūtra*:
'The bodhisattva has previously cultivated and accumulated roots of goodness that are associated with afflictions.'"
What are called the perfection of great compassion and so forth—these wholesome dharmas are termed "afflictions," yet they are not other afflictions.
It is based on these afflictions that one remains in the world to transform sentient beings, because that which is sought has not yet reached its ultimate consummation.

For this reason, although both have likewise abandoned all afflictions such as the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the bodhisattva does not regress from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), whereas the śrāvaka regresses.
As stated in the *Āyuṣmat-anavatapta-nāgarāja-sūtra*, the Buddha told the Naga King:
"The stage realized by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is a supramundane dharma, yet it is not separate from the mundane world."
"O Dragon King!
There is the samādhi of the noble wisdom of skillful means and prajñā; this is called the supramundane stage of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
O Dragon King!"
For example, just as a śrāvaka who enters the stage of a śrāvaka is called a srotāpanna and does not fall into the evil realms,
O Dragon King,
it is the same for a bodhisattva: upon entering the stage of a bodhisattva, they are called an avaivartika bodhisattva and do not fall into the evil realms.
“O Dragon King! Śrāvakas do not sever their afflictions when they attain the stage of a śrāvaka, because they have not yet transcended the state of non-sovereignty when they obtain the first fruit.”
O Dragon King!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas transcend the stage of the śrāvaka and realize the stage of a bodhisattva; therefore, they do not take up the minor fruit of the śrāvaka, but rather take up the fruit of great bodhi at the site of enlightenment.
For this reason, the śrāvakas are limited, while the bodhisattvas are immeasurable. "O Dragon King!

Suppose there were two people who both fell from a high mountain; one of them was brave, strong, and possessed great power, having previously practiced and mastered various skills, so that by means of skillful wisdom he climbed back to the mountain peak."

The second person’s physical strength was slight; he had not previously practiced various skills and lacked skillful wisdom, so having fallen at the foot of that mountain, he was unable to climb back up.
"O Dragon King!

In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates all phenomena as empty, signless, wishless, and unconditioned; relying on the power of prajñā, he observes sentient beings and dwells upon the summit of the mountain of all-knowledge."
"Furthermore, there is a sutra that says: 'Venerable Subhūti!

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva severs immeasurable afflictions such as the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), yet does not take up the minor fruits of the śrāvakas; instead, they take up the fruit of the great bodhi of all Buddhas. Observing all Buddha-dharmas, with a heart of great compassion they take pity on all sentient beings, cultivating the bodhisattva practices and severing all afflictions such as the view of a self-existent body.'"
Therefore, one does not take up the minor fruit of the śrāvaka, but rather takes up the great fruit of the bodhi of all Buddhas.
Subhūti addressed Mañjuśrī, saying: "Mañjuśrī!..."

This matter is rare: this person who is a Bodhisattva through great skillful means has severed all afflictions, such as the view of a self-identity, yet is able to refrain from taking the lesser fruit of a Śrāvaka.
Mañjuśrī said: "Virtuous Subhūti!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses the nature of wisdom encompassed by great skillful means; therefore, although the bodhisattva knows all afflictions such as the view of a self-body as they truly are, he is able to refrain from taking up the minor fruits of the śrāvakas."
"Venerable Subhūti! It is as if a strong man were to take a sharp-edged blade and cut down a śāla tree; that śāla tree would remain standing and not fall.
Venerable Subhūti!"

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is likewise so: possessing the nature of great skillful means and the wisdom of prajñā, the Bodhisattva severs all afflictions such as the view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi), yet is able to refrain from taking up the minor fruits of the śrāvaka.

“‘Venerable Subhūti! When those śāla trees, at another time, encounter the moisture of rain from the heavens, they immediately sprout branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits once more, becoming fully restored as they were before for the enjoyment of sentient beings.’”
Venerable Subhūti! It is likewise for the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva:

having been moistened by the rain of the great mind of loving-kindness and compassion, although they have severed the afflictions such as the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), they enter the triple world through skillful means to manifest birth in worldly families, conforming to the enjoyments of all sentient beings.
“‘Venerable Subhūti! Furthermore, at a later time, those śāla trees were blown and shaken by a great wind, whereupon they fell to the ground and never grew again.’”

Venerable Subhūti! It is likewise with the bodhisattva mahāsattva: blown by the fierce winds of great wisdom, they are forever extinguished and no longer arise within the ground of the site of enlightenment.

"Therefore, since the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva first resolved his mind [on enlightenment], all his mental activities have been different from those of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, because the dharmas of the mental activities of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are fundamentally different from theirs.
If they were identical in every respect, then Śrāvakas would become Bodhisattvas and Bodhisattvas would become Śrāvakas."

Question: "Just as a śrāvaka first abandons the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and subsequently gradually abandons the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), why does the bodhisattva not follow the same procedure as the śrāvaka by first abandoning the afflictions of the path of seeing and only thereafter abandoning the afflictions of the path of cultivation?"
He asked again:

"If a bodhisattva takes up residence for immeasurable eons and cultivates and accumulates immeasurable roots of goodness, why do those such as the srotāpannas not take up residence for immeasurable eons, nor cultivate and accumulate immeasurable roots of goodness?"

He replied: "Because those such as the *srotāpanna* constantly possess a mind that delights in severing afflictions, because they have attained the untainted light of the antidote, and because they grow increasingly fearful of all worldly existence, they give rise to this thought:
'When shall I attain liberation from all suffering and enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder?'"
Therefore, within the path of cultivation, the remaining afflictions naturally and gradually exhaust themselves.
For this reason, the śrāvaka does not take up dwelling for immeasurable eons, nor do they cultivate and accumulate immeasurable roots of goodness.
For immeasurable eons, the Bodhisattva has acted as a cause for the benefit of all sentient beings and performed deeds for their welfare, thereby attaining such ultimate resolve.

Furthermore, one perceives the Tathatā and the nectar-like Dharma-realm, and observes that the bodies of all sentient beings are in reality no different from the state sought by oneself; therefore, because all afflictions that obstruct the bodhisattva’s practice of benefiting sentient beings are seen within the path of cultivation, they are severed simultaneously within the path of seeing.

Furthermore, by observing that the happiness of benefiting all sentient beings is superior to the happiness of nirvana, the bodhisattva takes up dwelling in the world for immeasurable eons to cultivate all practices; because they are able to see clearly through the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), they cultivate and accumulate immeasurable roots of merit for enlightenment to attain the benefit of great enlightenment, and thus they cultivate and accumulate immeasurable roots of goodness.

Question: "If a bodhisattva, upon seeing that the afflictions of the path of cultivation can obstruct the practice of benefiting sentient beings, eliminates them within the path of seeing for this reason, why does he not suppress the afflictions of the path of cultivation with mundane wisdom while in the path of seeing?"

He replied: "The distancing from all afflictions (*kleśa*) is called the cause of non-retrogression. If one were to see the Dharma apart from the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), or if one were to sever all afflictions apart from the untainted path, then such an objection could be raised: 'Why does the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*) not subdue the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga-kleśa*)? [But since this is not the case, the objection does not hold]."
If the worldly path were identical to the worldly path, it would lack such power; therefore, one cannot say that [the practitioner] is non-retrogressive.

However, when this bodhisattva, upon the very moment of seeing the path, forever severs all dharmas that are to be remedied and attains great compassion and so forth, giving rise to the ultimate bodhicitta, he is called a non-retrogressive bodhisattva.
One should know this!

Therefore, the Bodhisattva perceives phenomena as they truly are and accomplishes skillful means; he does not take up the stages of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha. Perceiving and knowing all the various faults and afflictions of the world as they truly are, he performs worldly activities for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings; he does not abandon the world, yet he is not defiled by the faults and afflictions of the world.
"Therefore, the noble Mañjuśrī addressed the sons of heaven, saying: 'O sons of heaven!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not abide in the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), nor do they abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); for this reason, bodhisattvas are called fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).'"

Why is this? Because the bodhisattva is detached from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and does not abide in unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*). He knows that conditioned phenomena have faults and knows that unconditioned phenomena are faultless.
Because he knows all faults, he does not abide in the conditioned.
They know the unconditioned dharma, yet they do not dwell in the unconditioned.
O sons of the gods!
It is like a powerful athlete shooting an arrow upward into the sky; that arrow, having no support or dwelling place in the midst of space, does not fall to the ground.
"O sons of the gods!
This matter is difficult, yet there is something even more difficult.
The sons of the gods addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Such a matter is rare and most difficult; there is nothing more difficult than this.
Mañjuśrī said to the devaputra:

"The difficult deeds performed by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas exceed even this, for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas realize the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) without abandoning the conditioned (saṃskṛta), and they are able to teach and transform those who have fallen into the conditioned without themselves falling into the conditioned."
Question: “Regarding those who are ultimately destined (*niyata*), the Tathāgata has said in the sūtras:

‘If a śrāvaka is ultimately destined, having distanced himself from the three fetters (*trisaṃyojana*), he attains the stage of stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) and does not fall into the evil realms; after seven more births among humans and devas, he will forever be free from all suffering and ultimately realize the path of arhatship.’”
“The Bodhisattva is likewise; having severed the three fetters and so forth, for what reason does he dwell for immeasurable eons unlike the Śrāvakas?
He replied: “This interpretation is not correct.”

Why is this? That which is called "ultimate certainty" is spoken of according to the sūtras of the Śrāvaka vehicle; however, for a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, it is by relying on immeasurable practices and seeking all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) that the pure supramundane path can purify omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
The Mahāyāna sūtras state:
"For this reason, the bodhisattva takes up [the vow] to dwell for immeasurable eons. It is asked:
"This meaning is not so. Why is this?

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva of the first stage were to distance themselves from all remedial dharmas and attain ultimate non-retrogression regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, for what reason does the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-bodhicitta-sūtra* state: "..."?

"The first resolve, the initial arousal of the mind, can transcend the stage of the śrāvaka; the second resolve, the arousal of the mind through practice, can transcend the stage of the pratyekabuddha; the third resolve, the non-retrogressive arousal of the mind, transcends the stage of indetermination; and the fourth resolve, the arousal of the mind of the single-birth-to-enlightenment, abides securely in the stage of determination."

He replied: "In that sutra, it is based on the realization of the stages of superior progress, based on the distancing from the factors to be abandoned within the intermediate stage, and based on the transcendence of the indeterminate stages in the successive higher stages; therefore, this statement does not contradict that sutra."
What is the meaning of this?
It is like the remedial factors of the first dhyāna.
What does this clarify?

Just as followers of the Hīnayāna are said to abandon the indeterminate causes—the afflictions of the desire realm to be abandoned through the path of cultivation—within the preliminary dhyāna (anāgamya), and are likewise said to abandon the afflictions of the path of cultivation within the fourth dhyāna, this is not contradictory because they employ progressively superior remedial methods at each successive stage.
Why is this? It is because they serve as antidotes to causes such as [regression].

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is likewise: in the first stage (*bhūmi*), he abandons the causes of regression that are contrary to the bodhicitta, namely all afflictions such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Because he achieves the practice of the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*) and so forth, he ultimately remains far removed from the causes for regressing from the bodhicitta. Thus, up to the eighth stage, he attains the superior, progressive, and most distant antidotes; this is called "transcending the stages of uncertainty and abiding in the stages of certainty."

Because they possess the dharmas that serve as antidotes and because they are the cause of meditative concentration, the statement that one "transcends the stage of non-concentration" (aniyata-bhūmi) is not contradictory in meaning.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "transcending the stage of non-concentration": because the aspiration for the great nirvāṇa of the Buddha’s bodhi has not yet been severed, the exhaustion resulting from the effort exerted in performing various practices is termed the "cause of non-concentration. Therefore, it is only from the eighth stage upward that one is said to have transcended the stage of non-concentration.
What is the meaning of this?
It is as in the passage concerning the transcendence of suffering and so forth in that context. What does this clarify?

In the Hīnayāna, one becomes weary of and transcends the suffering of the desire realm; yet, although one has become weary of and transcended the suffering of the desire realm, one has not yet transcended the causes of suffering such as consciousness within the stage of the first dhyāna. Because one has not yet transcended the factors to be remedied (*vipakṣa-dharma*), the Tathāgata stated in the sūtras that one transcends suffering within the second dhyāna.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Where does the faculty of sorrow (daurmanasyendriya) cease?
The Buddha replied:
"It ceases within the first dhyāna.
He asked again:
"Where does the faculty of suffering cease?"
The Buddha said:
"It ceases within the second dhyāna.
He asked again:
"Where does the faculty of joy (sukhendriya) cease?
The Buddha said,
"It ceases within the third dhyāna."
He asked again:
"Where does the faculty of pleasure cease?
The Buddha said:
"It ceases within the fourth dhyāna.

Thus, although one transcends all marks of form and so forth at the time of the first dhyāna through such weariness, it is said that one transcends them in the fourth dhyāna because it is the cause of that weariness and transcendence.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is likewise: having already transcended the stage of uncertainty (*aniyata-bhūmi*) within the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), from the second stage upward through the seventh stage, because the aspiration for the Buddha’s enlightenment and great *nirvāṇa* has not yet been severed, the effortful application of the practices initiated therein is termed the "stage of uncertainty. Therefore, because that [effort] is the cause of an uncertain mind that is not yet fulfilled, it is stated that one transcends the stage of uncertainty within the eighth stage; thus, the statements are not contradictory.

Furthermore, because they have attained the complete and perfect convergence of the causes and conditions for ultimate bodhicitta, it is said that their initial generation of the mind surpasses the stage of the śrāvakas.
As the Tathāgata said in the *Dharmamudrā-sūtra*: "Maitreya!..."
There are seven causes for generating the bodhicitta. What are these seven?
First, generating the bodhicitta through the transformative teachings of the Buddhas.
Second, generating the bodhicitta upon seeing that the Dharma is about to perish;
third, generating the bodhicitta by giving rise to great compassion for all sentient beings;
fourth, generating the bodhicitta through the Bodhisattva’s transformative teachings.
Fifth, they give rise to the bodhicitta because of practicing giving;
sixth, they give rise to the bodhicitta by learning from others;
seventh, they give rise to the bodhicitta upon hearing the description of the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.

“Maitreya! Those who develop the bodhicitta through the teachings and transformations of the Buddhas; those who develop the bodhicitta upon seeing that the Dharma is about to perish; and those who develop the bodhicitta by giving rise to great compassion for all sentient beings—these three types of generating the mind can protect the True Dharma and swiftly achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. The other four ways of generating the mind do not constitute true bodhisattvas; they cannot uphold the True Dharma of the Buddhas nor swiftly achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
What does this clarify?

It means that if a bodhisattva accomplishes the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*) and never regresses, attaining the great power of courageous vigor through the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and—being pierced by the arrows of transgression from all sentient beings in the world—contemplates those beings and gives rise to great kindness and compassion, thereby gathering and increasing all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), it is said that at the moment of first generating the mind of awakening (*prathamacittotpāda*), one transcends the stage of the śrāvaka.

Regarding the second point, that the arousal of the mind surpasses the stage of the pratyekabuddha: a person who is a pratyekabuddha, being superior to a śrāvaka, ultimately does not act for the sake of others, but rather seeks quiescent nirvāṇa solely for their own sake.

When a bodhisattva first observes the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and contemplates the supreme patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they have not yet attained the path beyond the indeterminate; however, because they are able to transcend all arising thoughts as well as the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, it is said that the second arousal of the mind transcends the stage of the pratyekabuddha.

Regarding the statement that "the third arousal of the mind transcends the stage of non-fixity": because within the first stage one abandons the causes of non-fixity and attains the causes of fixity, all instances of generating the mind transcend the stage of non-fixity; therefore, it is said that the third arousal of the mind transcends the stage of non-fixity.

Regarding the fourth, "arousing the mind to abide in the stage of meditative concentration": from the second bhūmi upward, one is far removed from all factors to be abandoned (*vipakṣa*); therefore, because one abides in the stage of ultimate concentration, it is said that the fourth is "arousing the mind to abide in the stage of meditative concentration."

"Furthermore, regarding one who does not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*: when a bodhisattva attains freedom from those factors that are contrary to the arousal of the bodhicitta, they are called a non-regressing bodhisattva."
As it is said in the *Ratnadārikā-sūtra*: "O Ratnadārikā!
There are thirty-two obstructive barriers and paths that oppose the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva."
What are these thirty-two?
First, those who seek the vehicle of the śrāvaka;
second, those who seek the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha;
Third, seeking the realms of Śakra and Brahmā;
fourth, relying upon and becoming attached to the place of one's birth while practicing the pure conduct of brahmacarya;
fifth, single-mindedly regarding the roots of virtue as "mine."
Sixth, if one becomes stingy, greedy, and possessive toward wealth and treasures once they have been acquired;
